cells.tense: You're standing in the middle of a clearing you didn't have to force, and you know how you got here.
cells.ask: Offer the quiet practice one more day than feels necessary, and let repetition, not worry, do the refining.
cells.core:
It all came down on its own because you finally stopped believing the story that held it up, and you didn't panic — you just watched the walls go. You know what matters without having to argue it through first, and you trust that knowing, which is why you keep clearing space for the next true thing.

What keeps this open is small and dull on purpose: the same practice, the same hour, kept up whether or not you feel inspired. Nothing dramatic — just showing up for the discipline of it, day after day, until the refining happens in you the way it happens in a garden when nobody's watching.
cells.sheetLine: You know what matters, and you're not forcing the clearing.
cells.verb: letting what can't hold give way, all at once
cells.place: where you know what's worth your attention before you can explain why

cells.tense: You're bracing for the next thing to fall before it's even wobbled.
cells.ask: Teach one piece of what you know to one person, slow, out loud — and let the teaching bend to them.
cells.core:
You've got a hammer out and you're swinging at anything with a seam. Every structure looks like it's about to betray you, so you're tearing ahead of the tearing, calling it freedom when it's mostly noise. The clearing has turned into a habit of clearing, and nothing gets to stand long enough to be lived in.

What settles the pace is handing what you know to someone else. Meaning passed person to person has a tempo you can't rush; you can't teach anyone by knocking their walls down for them. Stay in it with another person, adapting what you know so it lands in a life that isn't yours, and the swinging quiets down into something that carries.

cells.tense: You're holding up the walls that already came down and pretending you still hear the roof.
cells.ask: Build one small structure that makes your week make sense — a schedule, a rule for yourself, a clear container — and let it serve the thing it's holding.
cells.core:
You know the thing is dead. You knew it before you started holding it up, and you've been holding it up anyway, arms shaking, telling yourself it just needs a little more time. The knowing is there; the letting-fall isn't. The truth already arrived and you're still sweeping around it.

What's missing isn't insight. It's a container with actual walls. Give the week a shape — a time it starts, a line you don't cross, a rule you keep not because it's strict but because it makes the rest of life navigable. Structure that serves what it organizes is what lets you finally put down what you've been carrying, and put it down in a room you built.

cells.tense: You're walking around in a building that's already come down and describing it like you're still inside it.
cells.ask: Let yourself move toward one thing you actually want this week — one small step, chosen from genuine wanting, not from ought.
cells.core:
There's a truth you already know and haven't said, and it's quietly running your attention, sorting what you notice and what you skip. You'd describe it as just being how things are. But something in you has already chosen, already cleared, already started moving — and you're narrating it like you're reading it off a page.

When it's working here, there's a clean pull forward: you want a thing, you take a step, and the wanting and the walking are the same motion. That's what to reclaim. Pick one thing you actually want this week and let yourself go toward it, small, without needing to know yet why it matters. Direction from feeling is the simplest form of the knowing you've been denying is yours.
